reference.source: Kaplan & Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry; DSM-5-TR
clinicalPearls: Characterised by restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight, intense fear of weight gain, and a disturbance in how body weight or shape is experienced
Two patterns are recognised: a restricting type and a binge-eating/purging type
Physical consequences include amenorrhoea, bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, lanugo hair, and osteopenia
Purging behaviours can cause electrolyte disturbances such as hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis, and dental erosion
Management principles centre on structured nutritional rehabilitation and weight restoration alongside psychotherapy, with family-based treatment favoured for adolescents
Medical stabilisation takes priority in severe cases; feeding must be advanced cautiously to avoid refeeding syndrome
Comorbid depression, anxiety, and obsessive-compulsive features are common, and suicide risk is elevated
Weigh patients and monitor electrolytes and cardiac status, since bradycardia and QT prolongation can be dangerous
reference.pathophysiology: Anorexia nervosa arises from an interaction of genetic and temperamental vulnerability (perfectionism, anxiety, harm avoidance), sociocultural pressures, and neurobiological factors including altered reward and interoceptive processing and serotonergic and dopaminergic dysregulation. Starvation itself perpetuates the disorder through neuroendocrine and cognitive changes, and complications reflect the systemic effects of chronic malnutrition.
additionalDifferentials: Major depressive disorder with appetite loss
Malignancy or chronic infection causing weight loss
additionalInvestigations: Weight, height, and body mass index with growth trajectory in young people
Electrolytes including potassium, phosphate, and magnesium
ECG to assess for bradycardia and QT prolongation
Full blood count, renal and liver function, and glucose
Bone density assessment in prolonged illness
Assessment for refeeding risk before and during nutritional rehabilitation
redFlags: Severe bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, or arrhythmia indicating cardiac instability
Dangerous electrolyte derangement, particularly hypokalaemia and hypophosphataemia
Rapid or extreme weight loss and very low body mass index
reference.prognosis: Anorexia nervosa has one of the highest mortality rates among psychiatric disorders, from both medical complications and suicide. Many patients recover, particularly with early intervention in adolescence, but a substantial proportion follow a chronic or relapsing course.
pitfalls: Refeeding too rapidly and precipitating life-threatening refeeding syndrome
Focusing on weight alone while neglecting electrolyte and cardiac monitoring
Being reassured by a normal weight in the binge-purge type despite dangerous electrolyte disturbance
Delaying medical stabilisation while awaiting psychiatric transfer
management: Make structured nutritional rehabilitation and weight restoration the cornerstone of care, advancing feeding cautiously to avoid refeeding syndrome
Prevent refeeding syndrome by monitoring and replacing phosphate, potassium, and magnesium and giving thiamine before and during refeeding
Deliver psychological therapy, with family-based treatment favoured for adolescents and specialist eating-disorder-focused therapy for adults
Medically stabilise severe cases with attention to bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, and electrolyte disturbances such as hypokalaemia
Address bone health with attention to osteopenia and adequate calcium and vitamin D
Treat comorbid depression and anxiety and monitor suicide risk, recognising no drug is a primary treatment
Manage through a multidisciplinary team and consider inpatient or compulsory treatment when the illness is life-threatening
